teaser: A dozen people, one tiny boat, a pancake on a string, and nobody steering.
review_notes:
The hanging object is usually described as a pancake or cake on a string; kept as 'pancake'.
Panel about 58 x 33 cm.
Reconstruction: Ship of Fools and the Yale 'Allegory of Gluttony and Lust' formed one wing, 'Death and the Miser' (Washington) the other, 'The Wayfarer' (Rotterdam) the outside; based on tree-ring study of the wood.
Sebastian Brant's Ship of Fools, Basel 1494, and its possible link to the painting.
Gift to the Louvre in 1918 (Camille Benoit) and 'only Bosch in the Louvre'.
Date: catalog gives 1500; scholars generally place it c. 1490-1510.
Meaning of the crescent on the pennant and of the owl is debated; text says so.

lesson.text: Four mouths are wide open. A nun, a monk and the men behind them all strain toward a pancake that swings on a string between their faces. Nobody has bitten it yet. One more second and somebody's teeth will close, the cake will spin away, and the boat will rock. Hieronymus Bosch stops the game right here.

It is a party game: hands off, catch the food with your mouth. Bosch paints it on a boat no bigger than a bathtub, loaded with about a dozen people. A whole tree has been tied up as a mast. No one is holding a rudder. Start with the players.

lesson.title: The game
lesson.text: The center of the boat, around the plank that serves as a table.

spots.title: The pancake
spots.text: A pale disc hanging from a cord that runs up toward the mast. It is the exact center of the group. Everything in the boat points at something to eat.

spots.title: The nun
spots.text: Veiled, mouth open, and playing a lute. She belongs to a religious order sworn to a sober life. For Bosch's viewers the lute was an instrument of flirting and love songs.

spots.title: The monk
spots.text: Shaved head, gray robe, face tilted up at the cake across from her. A man of the church and a woman of the church, singing nose to nose over a snack.

spots.title: The table
spots.text: A plate of cherries and a cup sit on the plank. Cherries were a familiar hint at pleasures of the body. Nobody looks at them: there is something new to grab.

lesson.text: So this is no innocent picnic. Bosch lived in a town full of monasteries, and people there complained loudly about monks and nuns who ate, drank and sang better than they prayed. He puts two of them at the heart of his boat, but he lets everyone else on board behave just as badly.
His real name was Jheronimus van Aken. He signed his pictures “Bosch” after his hometown, 's-Hertogenbosch in the Netherlands, where he spent nearly all his life.

The idea of a boat full of fools was in the air. In 1494 a writer named Sebastian Brant published a long satirical poem, The Ship of Fools, in which every kind of human silliness boards a ship bound for a fools' paradise. It was a bestseller, illustrated and translated across Europe.
A fool, for Bosch's time, was not someone stupid. It was anyone who lives for the next bite and forgets where the boat is going. The painting is a sermon disguised as a joke.
A real fool is on board too, the professional kind, in costume. He is easier to find than the other watcher Bosch has hidden, much higher up, who sees the whole scene from above.
A pale face peers out of the leaves, far above the party. Where?

spots.title: The owl
spots.text: A small owl sits in the treetop that crowns the mast. In Bosch's pictures owls often stand watch over human folly. Whether it means wisdom or something darker is still argued.

lesson.text: From the owl down, the mast is a ladder of bad ideas. Bosch fills the edges of the boat with small scenes, each one a different way of losing your head. This is where the picture rewards slow looking.

spots.title: The jester
spots.text: Sitting alone on a branch in his fool's hood with ass's ears, sipping from a bowl. The one official fool is the quietest person here, and turns his back on the rest.

spots.title: The roast goose
spots.text: A plucked, roasted bird is tied to the mast. A man climbs up from the bushes with a long knife to cut it loose.

spots.title: The pennant
spots.text: A long pink flag curls in the wind, marked with a crescent moon. Its meaning is debated. It may hint at lunacy, the old idea that the moon turns people mad.

spots.title: Seasick
spots.text: At the stern a man leans over the side and throws up. Next to the barrel, the price of the party.

spots.title: The oar
spots.text: Look at what one passenger is using as an oar: a giant kitchen ladle. This boat is rowed with cooking tools.

spots.title: The jug
spots.text: On the left a hooded woman lifts a jug over a man slumped in the bottom of the boat, who clutches a flask on a cord trailing in the water.

spots.title: The swimmers
spots.text: Two naked men have left the boat and swim alongside. One holds up a bowl, begging for a refill.

spots.title: The fish
spots.text: A dead fish dangles from a bare branch at the back. Fish was the food for fasting days. Here it hangs ignored.

lesson.text: All of this is painted thinly and fast on a panel of oak only about 58 centimeters tall (23 inches). In places you can see the brush dragging pale paint across the sky. Bosch draws with the tip of the brush, like a cartoonist, where his fellow painters polished every surface smooth.

The painting is a fragment. Long ago, a taller panel was sawn in two. The lower piece, showing a fat man riding a barrel in the water, is now at Yale University in the United States. The cut runs just under the swimmers.

The story goes further. Tree-ring study of the wood suggests that this panel was one wing of a triptych, a painting in three hinged parts. The matching wing, a dying miser tempted by a bag of gold, is in Washington. The center panel is lost.
It is the only painting by Bosch in the Louvre. The museum received it as a gift in 1918.

So gluttony sat on one side and greed on the other, with something missing in the middle that we can only guess at. Go back to those four open mouths. The cake is still swinging, and the boat is still not going anywhere.

quiz.question: What are the nun and the monk trying to do?
options: Bite a pancake hanging on a string
quiz.explanation: They play a game of catching hanging food with the mouth.

quiz.question: What serves as the boat's mast?
quiz.explanation: A leafy tree is lashed upright, with an owl in its top.

quiz.question: Who wrote the satirical poem The Ship of Fools in 1494?
quiz.explanation: Brant's poem was a bestseller across Europe.

quiz.question: What is one passenger using as an oar?
quiz.explanation: The boat is rowed with a kitchen ladle.

quiz.question: Why is the painting called a fragment?
options: It was sawn from a taller panel
quiz.explanation: The lower part was cut off and is now at Yale.

quiz.question: Where does the professional fool sit?
quiz.explanation: The jester sits apart on a branch with his back to the party.

facts.text: Bosch took his name from his hometown.
facts.explanation: He was Jheronimus van Aken of 's-Hertogenbosch.

facts.text: Someone at the back of the boat is steering carefully with a rudder.
facts.explanation: No one steers; a passenger paddles with a ladle.

facts.text: The panel was originally the center of a triptych.
facts.explanation: It was part of a wing; the center panel is lost.
